chapter_theme: Friendship as a rare achievement and the strongest guard. It grows with use, lives in the heart rather than on the face, corrects as well as comforts, and moves to help as instinctively as a hand to a slipping garment.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: its importance (781), the reasons for it (782-783), its use (784), its chief cause (785), and its marks (786-790).

781.reading: What is as hard to make as friendship, and what guard is as hard for hostile deeds to get past?
781.nuance: The two questions are linked: the difficulty of getting it is the reason for its value as protection. Parimelazhagar opens by classifying friendship as natural or made and says this chapter treats the made kind, kin being treated elsewhere.

782.reading: Friendship with the good grows like the crescent moon filling, and that of fools shrinks like the moon after it is full.
782.nuance: The moon's phases make growth depend on the starting point: the good begin small and fools begin large. Parimelazhagar's reason is knowledge. Each pair at first doesn't know the other and later does, and it is that knowing which makes one friendship grow and the other shrink.

783.reading: The more it is practised, the bond with people of character is like the more a book is studied, its nayam.

positions.position: Nayam is delight: both friendship and study give increasing pleasure.
positions.quote: நூற் பொருள் கற்குந்தோறும் கற்றார்க்கு இன்பஞ் செய்தலை ஒக்கும்.

positions.position: The gain is understanding: a friend of good character teaches as a book does.
positions.quote: இது குணவானோடு நட்புக் கொள்ளின், அறிவுண்டா மென்றது.

784.reading: Friendship is not for laughing together, but for going ahead to rebuke when one oversteps.
784.nuance: மேற்சென்று has timing in it. The rebuke goes out before the wrong is done, says Parimelazhagar, and it is harsh because sweet words will not turn the person back. This is not a claim that friends should never laugh, only that laughter isn't the purpose.

785.reading: Neither meeting nor long acquaintance is needed; a shared feeling alone gives the claim of friendship.
785.nuance: Parimelazhagar's example is Kopperuncholan and Pisirandaiyar, who never met and whose bond was so close that one died with the other. The verse itself offers no example and says nothing of dying together.

786.reading: Friendship that makes the face smile is not friendship; friendship that makes the heart within smile is friendship.
786.nuance: The verse sounds as if the face doesn't matter. Parimelazhagar says that an implied 'also' is present, so both should bloom together. That softens a sharper opposition in the Tamil.

787.reading: Friendship turns one away from what destroys, sets one on the path, and in ruin shares the suffering.
787.nuance: The order is a plan of action: prevent, then guide, then, if all that fails, suffer alongside. Parimelazhagar adds that ruin in the third stage comes from a divine cause and so can't be averted. The verse names no such cause.

788.reading: Like the hand of a man whose garment slips, friendship clears away distress there and then.
788.nuance: The simile is about speed and also about no deliberation. Parimelazhagar notes that the hand gets there before the mind does. The garment also implies that the friend's trouble is a shame to be covered, and that the friend is as close as one's own limb.

789.reading: Where does friendship sit enthroned? In standing firm without wavering, supporting however one can.
789.nuance: ஒல்லும்வாய் sets a realistic limit: as far as one is able. The throne is unwavering support, not unlimited power. Parimelazhagar specifies support in virtue and wealth, which Pope follows in parentheses, while the verse itself gives no object.

790.reading: 'They are this to us and we are that to them': even when so adorned, friendship looks shabby.
790.nuance: A subtle point. For Parimelazhagar friendship has no 'I' and 'they', so that listing what each is to the other brings in a difference that did not exist. The praise itself is what damages it.

links.note: 448 says a king with no one to rebuke him falls even without enemies. 784 makes the same office of rebuke the very purpose of friendship. What a counsellor does for a ruler, a friend does for anyone.

783 says friendship grows with practice and 785 says practice isn't needed. Parimelazhagar reconciles them by ranking three causes of friendship and placing shared feeling first, but the verses themselves sit in plain tension.

785 makes acquaintance unnecessary, while a whole chapter on old friendship opens at 801. Parimelazhagar's gloss on 801 eases this by saying that பழைமை is not elapsed time but a certain kind of friendship.

Both liken a relationship to learning with a 'the more, the more' (-தொறும்). In 783 friendship deepens like study's delight, and in 1110 love with the beloved is like finding one's ignorance with each new thing learned. Learning gives the Kural its model of an inexhaustible bond.

source_issues: 785: Parimelazhagar's entry opens with his complete comment on 784 before reaching 785. Only the later part was used.
